nameStory: The rosy maple moth gets its charming name from its signature pink and yellow coloration that resembles the soft hues of a sunrise, combined with its strong connection to maple trees. The 'rosy' refers to the beautiful pink tones that can range from pale blush to vibrant magenta across its fuzzy wings and body.
description: The rosy maple moth is a small, incredibly fluffy moth that looks like a living cotton candy with its soft pink and yellow coloring. This adorable member of the giant silk moth family has a woolly, teddy bear-like body and wings that can vary from cream and white to bright pink and sunny yellow. Despite being called a 'giant' silk moth, it's actually one of the smaller members of its family. Adult moths don't eat at all, living only to mate and lay eggs.

idTips.label: Fuzzy pink and yellow coloration
idTips.description: Look for the unmistakable combination of pink and yellow hues that can range from soft pastels to vibrant cotton candy colors - no other New England moth has this distinctive color scheme

idTips.label: Woolly, teddy bear-like body
idTips.description: The body feels incredibly soft and fluffy to the touch, like a plush toy, and is noticeably furrier than most other moths you'll encounter

idTips.label: Male antennae
idTips.description: Males have thick, feathery antennae that look like tiny ferns or bottle brushes, much bushier than the thinner antennae of females

idTips.label: Size comparison
idTips.description: Though part of the 'giant' silk moth family, these are relatively small with a compact, rounded appearance rather than the massive wingspan of their cecropia moth cousins

idTips.label: Association with maples
idTips.description: Often found resting on or flying around maple trees during summer evenings, as this is their exclusive host plant

habitat: Rosy maple moths are found wherever maple trees grow throughout New England, from suburban neighborhoods with sugar maples lining the streets to mixed hardwood forests containing red and silver maples. They're equally at home in low-elevation areas and can be found up into the mountains wherever their host trees thrive. Look for them in parks, backyards, forest edges, and anywhere maple trees are abundant.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with the first individuals appearing in May. This is when you might spot the woolly pink and yellow adults resting on tree bark or flying toward lights at dusk.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season runs through summer when adults are most active and visible. Look for the distinctive greenstriped mapleworm caterpillars feeding on maple leaves, eating entire leaf blades and leaving behind just the stems.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down, and caterpillars prepare for winter by pupating in the soil. The bright green caterpillars with their distinctive stripes may still be visible on maple trees in early fall.
seasonality.winter: Moths overwinter as pupae buried in the soil beneath their host maple trees, remaining dormant until the following spring. No above-ground signs of the species are visible.

funFact: Despite being called 'giant silk moths,' adult rosy maple moths never eat a single meal in their entire adult lives - they survive solely on the energy they stored up as caterpillars, living just long enough to find a mate and reproduce!
confusionNotes: The rosy maple moth is virtually impossible to confuse with any other New England species thanks to its unique pink and yellow coloration - no other moth in our region sports this cotton candy color scheme. If you see pink and yellow together on a fuzzy moth, you've found a rosy maple moth!
contextualKnowledge: While called 'giant silk moths,' rosy maple moths are actually among the smallest members of the Saturniidae family, which can cause confusion for those expecting something massive. The 'giant' refers to the family as a whole, not this particular species.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus in New England, the rosy maple moth stands apart from other silk moths by its much smaller size and unique coloration. While its relatives like cecropia moths are truly giant with earth-tone colors, the rosy maple moth is compact and sports those unmistakable pink and yellow hues. Other silk moths in the region are typically brown, tan, or rust-colored rather than the rosy maple's distinctive pastel palette.
